subject: biology
title: Nerve Signaling
summary: Nerve signaling is the process by which a neuron picks up a stimulus, races an electrical impulse down its axon, hands the signal off chemically at the synapse, and triggers a response in the next cell. Follow the five-step chain from stimulus to response, see how myelin and saltatory conduction speed it up, and connect it back to the single neuron cell you already explored.

compareCandidate.label: Nerve signal vs. a phone call
compareCandidate.description: The electrical impulse racing down the axon is like a signal traveling through a wire, but crossing the synapse — where the signal must convert into a chemical, drift across a gap, and get picked up by a receiver — is like a phone converting your voice into a signal a tower has to catch and relay onward.

processes: Electrical impulse (action potential) conduction along the axon
Saltatory conduction at the nodes of Ranvier
Neurotransmitter release and diffusion across the synapse
Receptor binding on the postsynaptic neuron
Effector response (muscle contraction or gland secretion)
plainLanguageExplanation: A nerve signal is your body's version of a text message — but instead of Wi-Fi, it travels as a tiny electrical pulse racing down a thread-like cell called a neuron. When something touches your skin, hits your eye, or your brain decides to move a finger, a neuron flips into "on" mode for a split second, and that "on" state zips down its long tail (the axon) like a flame racing along a fuse. When the signal reaches the very end of the neuron, it can't jump the tiny gap to the next cell electrically — so it releases a burst of chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) that drift across the gap and dock onto the next neuron, restarting the electrical pulse all over again. Chain enough of these hand-offs together — skin to spinal cord to brain to muscle — and you get everything from flinching off a hot stove to reading this sentence.

keyFacts.label: Signal type
keyFacts.value: Electrical inside the neuron, chemical at the synapse (the gap between neurons)

keyFacts.label: Typical speed
keyFacts.value: Up to about 120 meters per second (over 250 mph) in fast, myelin-coated neurons

keyFacts.label: Chemical messenger
keyFacts.value: Neurotransmitters (e.g., acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin) carry the signal across the synapse

keyFacts.label: Speed booster
keyFacts.value: The myelin sheath insulates the axon and lets the impulse jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), speeding it up

keyFacts.label: Direction
keyFacts.value: Signals normally flow one way: dendrite to cell body to axon to synapse

keyFacts.label: Reset step
keyFacts.value: After firing, the neuron has a brief refractory period before it can fire again

whyItMatters: Every single thing you do — pulling your hand off something hot, catching a ball, laughing at a joke, remembering your locker combination — depends on nerve signals firing correctly and fast. Nerve signaling is also the reason medicine can help so many conditions: painkillers block pain signals, anesthesia pauses signaling during surgery, and conditions like multiple sclerosis (damaged myelin) or Parkinson's disease (low dopamine) happen when some part of this chain breaks down. Understanding nerve signaling is the foundation for understanding your brain, your reflexes, and how doctors treat nervous system disorders.
didYouKnow: The electrical impulse inside a neuron can't jump the gap to the next cell — it has to convert into a chemical messenger that drifts across the synapse, more like a relay handoff than one continuous wire.
compareReason: Nerve signaling and hormone signaling are the body's two communication systems: nerve signals are fast electrical impulses that trigger quick, short-lived responses, while hormone signals are slower chemical messengers that reach the whole body and often last much longer — complementary, not competing, ways the body coordinates itself.
